newsitem.title: UK: Tesco and Holiday Inn projects for N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Tesco and Holiday Inn projects for N.Ireland.

text.p: British mainland supermarket chain Tesco launched itself in Northern Ireland on Tuesday, opening a Belfast city centre "Metro" store with some 170 employees.

In another key service-sector development in the region, which is trying to shrug off the shadow of fresh guerrilla tension, Belfast businessman Diljit Rana announced the opening of his second Holiday Inn Hotel, the 114-bedroom "Holiday Inn Express", costing 4.5 million sterling.
Tesco's opening is seen by retail analysts as continuing evidence of faith by mainland-based chains in the region's growth potential.
But retail sources say local traders are concerned that "mainland giants" will eat into their market share. Some have challenged planning applications.

Work on a store for J. Sainsbury Plc, a rival operator to Tesco, was halted recently when courts upheld claims that the province's Department of Environment broke its own rules when it gave permission for the project.
Sainsbury is scheduled in December to open the first of seven province-wide supermarkets costing a total 100 million pounds.
It will be in Ballymena, County Antrim. The second, due to open next spring, is under construction at a prime Belfast commercial location.
"At the moment we have got planning applications in for two more stores, at Lisburn and Knocknagoney," Tesco Metro general manager in Belfast, David Arnold, told Reuters.
Asked if more were planned he replied: "It's really a question of whether we can get the sites."
"We would like to open more. We have not got specific locations. In terms of the public, they want us to open stores quickly. But in terms of the planning process, it is quite slow."
Arnold said the Metro-supermarket concept was designed to serve people who shop and work in the central city. There is a strong emphasis on fresh foods, he said.

Donald McFetridge, head of retail studies at the University of Ulster in Coleraine, County Londonderry, described the Tesco development -- which offers 12,000 product lines in a restored 130 years old landmark building -- as "a tremendous achievement".
"I think it is very good for the city centre," he told Reuters.
The Holiday Inn Express is being seen as a welcome increase in the capital's hotel-bedroom stock that was hit by closures during guerrilla bomb attacks in the early 1970s.
Earlier this year the province's burgeoning tourism trade was jolted by the collapse of an Irish Republican Army truce and heightened sectarian tension.
Tourism chiefs forecast a 100,000 reduction in visitor numbers that rocketed in 1995 as truces by rival guerrilla groups took hold.
The hotel is the latest venture by Rana, managing director of Andras House Ltd, which owns two other Belfast hotels, the Holiday Inn Garden Court and Renshaws.

The company, operating the hotels under a franchise from Holiday Inn Worldwide, plan to build two four-star Holiday Inn hotels, one on the outskirts of Belfast and the other near Larne, County Antrim.
